steps.prompt: What are the four categories in this survey?

steps.name: Organise the categories
steps.narration: Put similar responses in the same row. A clear frequency table has one row for each category.
steps.prompt: Which row would you use for each observation?

steps.name: Build tally groups
steps.narration: Count with four upright tally marks. The fifth crosses the four, making a group of five.
steps.prompt: Find a crossed group of five. Why is it faster to count?

steps.name: Write the frequencies
steps.narration: Frequency is how many observations are in each group. Count the tallies, including the cross-stroke.
steps.prompt: Compare each tally group with its number.

steps.name: Make the pictogram
steps.narration: Our pictogram key says one picture stands for two observations. One extra observation needs half a picture.
steps.prompt: Can you find an odd frequency and its half-picture?

steps.name: Read and check
steps.narration: Add the frequencies to check the total. The table and pictogram must represent the same data.
steps.prompt: Which category has the greatest frequency? Check the total.

steps.name: Read the collected data
steps.narration: We begin with a table of counts. Each category gets one bar. Every bar must use the same numerical scale.
steps.prompt: Which categories will appear along the bottom?

steps.name: Set a fair scale
steps.narration: Read the frequency axis first. For an ordinary bar chart, begin at zero and use equal-sized intervals.
steps.prompt: Where is zero, and what does one grid interval represent?

steps.name: Build the first bar
steps.narration: The first bar rises from zero to the first frequency, without crossing the category boundary.
steps.prompt: Read the first value using the y-axis.

steps.name: Build the second bar
steps.narration: Leave a clear gap. The height of the second bar, not its width or colour, shows its frequency.
steps.prompt: Is the second frequency larger or smaller?

steps.name: Complete the third bar
steps.narration: A third column uses the same scale. Changing the scale between columns would invalidate the comparison.
steps.prompt: Which of the first three columns is shortest?

steps.name: Complete the fourth bar
steps.narration: Four categories, four non-touching columns. Count the intervals to check the bar heights.
steps.prompt: How many observations are shown altogether?

steps.name: Find the important comparison
steps.narration: The marker identifies the tallest bar. Compare its value against the shortest bar and read the difference.
steps.prompt: How much higher is the tallest bar than the shortest?

steps.name: Interpret the chart carefully
steps.narration: Always check the vertical-axis baseline. If the chart starts above zero, the heights exaggerate small differences.
steps.prompt: How can a missing zero make a bar chart misleading?

steps.name: Read the source observations
steps.narration: We begin with measurements taken at equal time intervals. Each pair records a time and a measured value.
steps.prompt: Which quantity changes over time?

steps.name: Read both axes and the units
steps.narration: Time runs from left to right, with equal spacing. The measured quantity uses equally spaced values on the vertical axis.
steps.prompt: Which axis carries time, and which carries the measurement?

steps.name: Plot the first measured point
steps.narration: Go along to the first time, then up to its recorded value. Mark the exact intersection.
steps.prompt: How do both coordinates locate one observation?

steps.name: Plot the next point and join
steps.narration: Plot the second observation at its own time, then join the two readings with a straight line.
steps.prompt: Between these two observations, did the value rise or fall?

steps.name: Follow the third observation
steps.narration: The third point creates another line segment. Its steepness shows the rate of change between readings.
steps.prompt: Which interval so far has the greatest change?

steps.name: Trace the fourth observation
steps.narration: A new segment can rise, fall, or stay level. Reading the numbers matters more than the angle alone.
steps.prompt: Does the latest segment slope upward or downward?

steps.name: Connect every observed reading
steps.narration: Complete the series using real readings. A line graph connects measurements in their actual time order.
steps.prompt: Where is the highest observed point?

steps.name: Identify the turning point
steps.narration: The glowing marker identifies the highest observation. Trace the overall pattern from the first to the last time.
steps.prompt: When is the maximum, and does the series always rise?

steps.name: Interpret the trend and scale
steps.narration: Check the marked intervals and the labels. Cropping an axis changes the visual steepness but not the observations themselves.
steps.prompt: Would a cropped axis change any actual data values?

steps.name: Collect frequency data
steps.narration: A pie chart starts with counts. Each person or item belongs in exactly one category.
steps.prompt: What does one frequency count represent?

steps.name: Find the total frequency
steps.narration: Add every category. There are twenty responses in total. The whole circle represents those twenty responses.
steps.prompt: Why must all categories add to the same total?

steps.name: Convert frequency into angles
steps.narration: One response occupies eighteen degrees because three hundred and sixty degrees divided by twenty is eighteen.
steps.prompt: How many degrees does one response contribute?

steps.name: Draw the first sector
steps.narration: Multiply the frequency of the first category by the degrees per response. Draw that sector precisely.
steps.prompt: How does a larger frequency affect the sector angle?

steps.name: Build the second sector
steps.narration: Measure the second category angle. Begin its sector exactly where the first sector ends.
steps.prompt: Should sectors overlap or leave gaps?

steps.name: Draw the third sector
steps.narration: Convert the third category frequency into its correct angle. Its size remains proportional to the count.
steps.prompt: Does a count of four take one fifth of the circle?

steps.name: Complete the full circle
steps.narration: Complete the fourth sector. Every sector fits the circle, with no gaps or overlaps, and the angles total three hundred and sixty degrees.
steps.prompt: What total should the sector angles always have?

steps.name: Compare percentages
steps.narration: Convert each category into a percentage of all twenty responses, then check they total one hundred percent.
steps.prompt: Why do the percentages add up to one hundred?

steps.name: Read and check the chart
steps.narration: Read the coloured sectors alongside the frequency key. Check that all frequencies, angles and percentages agree.
steps.prompt: How can you check your finished pie chart?

steps.name: Collect continuous measurements
steps.narration: We have measurements recorded on a continuous scale. We need class boundaries so every observation is counted exactly once.
steps.prompt: What does a measurement tell us?

steps.name: Define class boundaries
steps.narration: These classes have different widths. Each value goes in one interval, including its lower boundary but excluding its upper boundary.
steps.prompt: Which class contains a value exactly on a boundary?

steps.name: Build the frequency table
steps.narration: Count every measurement once. The frequency tells us how many are in each class.
steps.prompt: Which column counts observations?

steps.name: Calculate class widths
steps.narration: Subtract the lower class boundary from the upper. These intervals do not all have the same width.
steps.prompt: How wide is the first class?

steps.name: Calculate frequency density
steps.narration: Divide frequency by class width. Frequency density is the correct vertical axis for a histogram with unequal class widths.
steps.prompt: How do you calculate the height of a bar?

steps.name: Build the histogram
steps.narration: The bars touch, and each bar stretches across its actual class interval. Its height is frequency density, not frequency.
steps.prompt: Which bars are wider?

steps.name: Verify bar area
steps.narration: A rectangle area is class width times frequency density. That area gives the frequency.
steps.prompt: How many observations does the widest bar represent?

steps.name: Read and compare
steps.narration: A tall narrow bar can contain fewer observations than a lower wide bar. Compare areas for frequency, not bar heights.
steps.prompt: Which bar has the largest area?

steps.name: Explain what the histogram means
steps.narration: A correct histogram has a continuous horizontal scale, bars that touch, and frequency density on the vertical axis. Area represents frequency.
steps.prompt: What is the difference between a histogram and a bar chart?

options: The vertical axis now starts at zero

steps.prompt: Who belongs to the population?

steps.narration: We record thirty in the first group, eighteen in the second and twelve in the third.

steps.prompt: Why might we use a sample?

steps.narration: In a simple random sample, every pupil should have an equal chance of selection.
steps.prompt: Could chance still produce an uneven sample?

steps.name: Compare the proportions
steps.narration: Compare the proportion in the sample with the proportion in the whole population.
steps.prompt: Are the proportions exactly the same?

steps.name: Use stratified sampling

steps.prompt: Why do proportional samples match the groups?

steps.name: See a convenient sample
steps.narration: If we ask only pupils in the final group, we fail to include the other groups.
steps.prompt: Who is missing from the sample?

steps.name: Identify the sampling bias
steps.narration: This convenience sample has a systematic bias. It does not represent the whole population.
steps.prompt: Is this evidence about everyone?

steps.prompt: How would you improve the survey?

steps.narration: Probability has a scale from zero to one. Zero means impossible; one means certain.

steps.name: Find its complement
steps.narration: The remaining seven outcomes are not green. Their probability is seven tenths, or zero point seven. Both probabilities total one.

steps.name: Justify your probability
steps.narration: The rule is favourable outcomes divided by all equally likely outcomes. Now try the model with eight tickets.

steps.narration: A fair spinner stops equally often in each equal-sized sector. Every sector represents one equally likely outcome.
steps.prompt: What tells us that the sectors are equally likely?

steps.name: Build an event
steps.narration: The chance of a win is the number of winning sectors divided by the number of equally likely sectors.
steps.prompt: Why would counting just the winning sectors be incomplete?

steps.name: Spin and observe
steps.narration: A single spin is uncertain. A spinner can stop in a winning sector or in another sector.
steps.prompt: Does one result tell us the exact chance of winning?

steps.name: Collect outcomes
steps.narration: Repeated spins give experimental relative frequency. The theoretical probability comes from the sector sizes.
steps.prompt: Why need not the experimental and theoretical values match after only a few spins?

steps.name: Predict a result

steps.name: Meet the apparatus
steps.narration: A fair die has six equally likely faces and a fair coin has two equally likely sides. Our apparatus shows these outcomes clearly.
steps.prompt: How many different faces can this die show?

steps.name: List possible outcomes
steps.narration: For a die and a coin, pair each of the six die numbers with heads and tails. That makes twelve equally likely pairs.
steps.prompt: Can you list the twelve outcomes without missing a pair?

steps.name: Choose a favourable event
steps.narration: An even number occurs on three faces. Heads occurs on one coin side. Three of the twelve pairs are favourable.
steps.prompt: Why are there three favourable pairs, not six?

steps.name: Observe one trial
steps.narration: A trial gives one result. A fair apparatus does not guarantee that a favourable event happens in any particular trial.
steps.prompt: Can you predict the next die and coin result with certainty?

steps.name: Collect the results
steps.narration: Count the favourable outcomes actually observed, and divide by the number of trials. This is experimental relative frequency.
steps.prompt: Why may observed frequency differ from theoretical probability?

steps.name: Compare and predict
steps.narration: Theoretical probability comes from all equally likely outcomes, while relative frequency comes from trials. Use larger experiments to investigate the difference.
steps.prompt: Which measurement should stay fixed as you run more trials?

steps.name: Watch the changing curve

steps.prompt: Does experimental probability always equal theoretical probability?

steps.name: Collect more evidence
steps.narration: Larger samples often give a steadier estimate. However, the experimental line need not get closer after every single new trial.
steps.prompt: Can the gap briefly increase, even after many trials?

steps.name: What makes a game fair?
steps.narration: A fair game gives neither side an advantage over many plays. We must compare the expected gross prize with the entry cost.
steps.prompt: Does winning half the time always mean a fair game?

steps.name: Count winning outcomes
steps.narration: The die has six equally likely outcomes. Two winning faces give a probability of two sixths, or one third.
steps.prompt: How many of the six faces win?

steps.name: Calculate the return
steps.narration: Multiply the probability of winning by the gross prize. With a three pound prize and one-third chance, the expected return is one pound.
steps.prompt: What is the expected prize return?

steps.name: Subtract the entry cost
steps.narration: The net expected gain is expected return minus the cost to enter. One pound minus one pound equals zero. That is a fair game.
steps.prompt: Why do we subtract the cost?

steps.name: Compare with simulated results
steps.narration: Run actual random games. Even for a fair game the total net gain may be above or below zero after a few trials.
steps.prompt: Does a fair game guarantee a break-even result after ten trials?

steps.name: Make the game unfair, then rebalance
steps.narration: Changing the number of winning faces or the prize changes expected value. To make the game fair, balance probability times gross prize with the entry cost.
steps.prompt: How can you make an unfair game fair?

steps.narration: An analogue clock has twelve hour numbers and sixty minute divisions. The hands do different jobs.
steps.prompt: Which hand travels furthest in one hour?
steps.say: The long hand reads minutes. The short hand reads hours, but it never jumps suddenly to the next number.

steps.name: Follow the short hand
steps.narration: The hour hand points to seven at seven o clock. It will gradually move toward eight as the minutes pass.
steps.prompt: Where does the short hand point at half past seven?
steps.say: The short hand travels thirty degrees in one hour, so it also moves half a degree per minute.

steps.name: Place the minute hand
steps.narration: Five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five. The long hand points at the five to show twenty-five minutes.
steps.prompt: Why does the number five indicate twenty-five minutes?
steps.say: Each labelled number represents five minutes for the long hand. Count five sets of five.

steps.name: Watch the hour move
steps.narration: At seven twenty-five, the hour hand is already past seven. It moves with every minute.
steps.prompt: Does the hour hand remain exactly on seven until eight o clock?
steps.say: After twenty-five minutes, the hour hand has moved twelve and a half degrees beyond seven.

steps.name: Read the time
steps.narration: The clock reads seven twenty-five. Both hands agree with that reading.
steps.prompt: Read the whole time aloud, including the minutes.
steps.say: Use the long hand to find minutes, then check where the short hand sits between the hours.

steps.name: Check the angles
steps.narration: Between each hour number is thirty degrees. Each minute is six degrees. At seven twenty-five the hour hand has moved from seven.
steps.prompt: How could you find an angle between the hands?
steps.say: Calculate each hand’s angle from twelve. Remember that the hour hand moves continuously, then compare.

steps.name: Read the route
steps.narration: A timetable has stops in rows and journeys in columns. Start by finding the departure stop.
steps.prompt: Which column stays with the same bus?
steps.say: Each column is one vehicle and one journey. You cannot mix its times with another bus.

steps.name: Choose the service
steps.narration: Service A leaves Maple Park at eight fifteen. Keep your finger on service A as you read down.
steps.prompt: Why is it wrong to jump from the A column to the B column?
steps.say: The service letter is your guide. Stay in the same column all the way to the destination.

steps.name: Locate departure
steps.narration: At Maple Park, service A departs at eight fifteen. Write the start time.
steps.prompt: What is the starting time for service A?
steps.say: Use the top stop row. Eight fifteen is the departure time, not the duration.

steps.name: Locate arrival
steps.narration: The same service reaches the Leisure Centre at eight fifty-eight. Keep the start and finish in the same column.
steps.prompt: Where is the arrival time in the A column?
steps.say: Follow the luminous journey trace down to Leisure Centre: eight fifty-eight.

steps.name: Calculate duration
steps.narration: Subtract eight fifteen from eight fifty-eight. The difference is forty-three minutes.
steps.prompt: How many minutes pass from fifteen minutes past eight to fifty-eight minutes past eight?
steps.say: These times are in the same hour, so subtract the minutes: fifty-eight minus fifteen.

steps.name: Check the journey
steps.narration: Forty-three minutes is the journey time. The answer is a duration, so it needs the unit minutes.
steps.prompt: Why must we put minutes after forty-three?
steps.say: Arrival time is a clock reading. Journey time is a duration: forty-three minutes.

steps.name: Read the hours and hourly rate
steps.narration: This payslip shows twelve hours at nine pounds and fifty pence per hour. First identify the pay rate and the hours worked.
steps.prompt: What would twelve hours of work at nine pounds fifty per hour earn?
steps.say: Multiply the hours by the hourly rate. Both numbers describe the same pay period.

steps.name: Calculate gross earnings
steps.narration: Twelve times nine pounds and fifty pence is one hundred and fourteen pounds. That is gross pay before anything is taken away.
steps.prompt: Why is gross pay not always the money you receive?
steps.say: Gross pay is what was earned before deductions. It is not the take-home amount.

steps.name: Identify the deduction
steps.narration: This example payslip has an eight-pound deduction. It is an illustrative charge, not a real tax calculation.
steps.prompt: What is a deduction?
steps.say: An amount taken off gross pay is a deduction. Keep it separate from everyday spending.

steps.name: Find take-home pay
steps.narration: Subtract the eight-pound example deduction from one hundred and fourteen pounds. The take-home pay is one hundred and six pounds.
steps.prompt: Which operation finds net pay?
steps.say: Gross minus deductions equals net pay. Here that is one hundred and six pounds.

steps.name: Allocate transport and lunch
steps.narration: Now set aside seventeen pounds for a bus pass and nine pounds for lunches. Together the budgeted spending is twenty-six pounds.
steps.prompt: Should we subtract expenses from gross or take-home pay?
steps.say: Spend from take-home pay. The payroll deduction has already been removed.

steps.name: Find money left and verify
steps.narration: One hundred and six pounds, minus twenty-six pounds, leaves eighty pounds unallocated. Check by adding back the twenty-six pounds spent.
steps.prompt: How can you check the remaining balance?
steps.say: Add spending back to the remaining amount. Eighty pounds plus twenty-six pounds returns to net pay.

steps.name: Begin with the capital
steps.narration: We are saving two hundred pounds at five percent a year. The original deposit is called the capital.
steps.prompt: What does five percent of two hundred pounds mean?
steps.say: Five percent means five in every hundred. Find that part of the original saving.

steps.name: Find one year of simple interest
steps.narration: Five percent of two hundred pounds is ten pounds. Simple interest adds ten pounds for each year.
steps.prompt: How much interest is earned in the first year?
steps.say: Two hundred pounds times five percent is ten pounds. The first year earns ten pounds.

steps.name: Repeat the same yearly gain
steps.narration: At two years, simple interest is twenty pounds. At three years, it is thirty pounds. The amount added each year stays ten pounds.
steps.prompt: Why are the cyan bars increasing at a steady pace?
steps.say: Simple interest always uses the starting amount, not last year’s total.

steps.name: Compare compounding
steps.narration: Compound interest is different: after year one, we calculate the next five percent from two hundred and ten pounds.
steps.prompt: What would five percent of two hundred and ten pounds be?
steps.say: With compounding, the next year can earn more because previous interest is included.

steps.name: Reveal the growing difference
steps.narration: Over five years the purple compound bars grow slightly faster. Look at how their height separates from the cyan bars.
steps.prompt: Which method begins to earn more interest over time?
steps.say: The gap grows because compound interest earns interest on earlier interest.

steps.name: Calculate, compare and verify
steps.narration: After five years, simple interest is fifty pounds. The compound gain, with annual penny rounding, is fifty-five pounds and twenty-seven pence.
steps.prompt: What must you add to either interest amount to find the final savings balance?
steps.say: Add the original two hundred pounds to the interest gained. Never confuse interest with final balance.

steps.name: Begin with the capital
steps.narration: We are saving two hundred pounds at five percent a year. The original deposit is called the capital.
steps.prompt: What does five percent of two hundred pounds mean?
steps.say: Five percent means five in every hundred. Find that part of the original saving.

steps.name: Find one year of simple interest
steps.narration: Five percent of two hundred pounds is ten pounds. Simple interest adds ten pounds for each year.
steps.prompt: How much interest is earned in the first year?
steps.say: Two hundred pounds times five percent is ten pounds. The first year earns ten pounds.

steps.name: Repeat the same yearly gain
steps.narration: At two years, simple interest is twenty pounds. At three years, it is thirty pounds. The amount added each year stays ten pounds.
steps.prompt: Why are the cyan bars increasing at a steady pace?
steps.say: Simple interest always uses the starting amount, not last year’s total.

steps.name: Compare compounding
steps.narration: Compound interest is different: after year one, we calculate the next five percent from two hundred and ten pounds.
steps.prompt: What would five percent of two hundred and ten pounds be?
steps.say: With compounding, the next year can earn more because previous interest is included.

steps.name: Reveal the growing difference
steps.narration: Over five years the purple compound bars grow slightly faster. Look at how their height separates from the cyan bars.
steps.prompt: Which method begins to earn more interest over time?
steps.say: The gap grows because compound interest earns interest on earlier interest.

steps.name: Calculate, compare and verify
steps.narration: After five years, simple interest is fifty pounds. The compound gain, with annual penny rounding, is fifty-five pounds and twenty-seven pence.
steps.prompt: What must you add to either interest amount to find the final savings balance?
steps.say: Add the original two hundred pounds to the interest gained. Never confuse interest with final balance.

steps.name: Name the three quantities
steps.narration: Distance is how far something travels. Speed tells us how far it travels in each hour. Time tells us how long the journey takes.
steps.prompt: Which quantity measures how far something goes?
steps.say: Distance, speed and time are connected; the triangle makes their relationship visible.

steps.name: Find what is missing
steps.narration: We know a train travels one hundred and fifty kilometres in two and a half hours. We want the speed in kilometres per hour.
steps.prompt: Which two values are already known?
steps.say: The distance is one hundred and fifty kilometres. The time is two and a half hours.

steps.name: Reveal the calculation
steps.narration: To find speed, use distance divided by time. The units become kilometres per hour.
steps.prompt: Why do we divide instead of multiply?
steps.say: Divide distance by time to find the distance travelled in each hour.

steps.name: Check the unit
steps.narration: We divide one hundred and fifty kilometres by two and a half hours. The distance per hour is our answer unit.
steps.prompt: What unit must speed have?
steps.say: Check the unit: kilometres per hour. Units tell us what the calculation means.

steps.name: Count up to the result
steps.narration: One hundred and fifty divided by two and a half is sixty. The speed is sixty kilometres per hour.
steps.prompt: Can you check by working backwards?
steps.say: Sixty kilometres each hour for two and a half hours gives one hundred and fifty kilometres.

steps.name: Generalise and transfer
steps.narration: To find the top quantity, multiply the two bottom quantities. To find either bottom quantity, divide the top by the other bottom.
steps.prompt: How would you find mass from density and volume?
steps.say: The same structure works for density and pressure. Keep your units consistent.

steps.name: Read the real-world situation
steps.narration: We want to estimate the mass of a school delivery. Each crate weighs nineteen point eight kilograms, and the plan is for six point one crates.
steps.prompt: What are the two quantities?
steps.say: Find what is being multiplied and keep the kilograms in mind.

steps.name: Choose useful rounded numbers
steps.narration: Nineteen point eight is close to twenty. Six point one is close to six.
steps.prompt: Why are twenty and six helpful?
steps.say: These friendly numbers are near the originals, without changing their place value.

steps.name: Put both values in the ring
steps.narration: Use twenty multiplied by six to estimate the shipment mass.
steps.prompt: Which operation belongs here?
steps.say: This is multiplication, because each crate adds about twenty kilograms.

steps.name: Keep the unit
steps.narration: The estimate will be measured in kilograms. A unit gives the approximate answer meaning.
steps.prompt: What will our answer unit be?
steps.say: Remember to write kilograms. A number without its unit is incomplete.

steps.name: Calculate the estimate
steps.narration: Twenty multiplied by six is one hundred and twenty kilograms. This is an estimate, not the precise mass.
steps.prompt: Is the result exact or approximate?
steps.say: About one hundred and twenty kilograms is a sensible prediction.

steps.name: Compare and transfer
steps.narration: The exact calculation gives a little more than our estimate. Estimation helps check whether a later exact result is reasonable.
steps.prompt: What would make a predicted mass ten times too large?
steps.say: Check the place value: one wrong zero can make a prediction ten times too large.

shopping.speech: A delivery contains about six crates at about twenty kilograms each. That is roughly one hundred and twenty kilograms.

steps.name: Start with a measurement
steps.narration: A length is given as twelve centimetres to the nearest centimetre. It might not have been exactly twelve centimetres.
steps.prompt: Does twelve centimetres describe one exact length?
steps.say: Rounded measurements stand for a whole interval, not just one exact value.

steps.name: Find the rounding increment
steps.narration: The rounding increment is one centimetre. Half of one centimetre is zero point five centimetres.
steps.prompt: What is half of the rounding increment?
steps.say: The halfway distance is half the step. Here that is half a centimetre.

steps.name: Find the lower endpoint
steps.narration: Take half a centimetre away from twelve. The lower bound is eleven point five centimetres and it is included.
steps.prompt: Is the lower endpoint part of the interval?
steps.say: Eleven point five rounds up to twelve, so the lower endpoint is included.

steps.name: Find the upper endpoint
steps.narration: Add half a centimetre to twelve. The upper bound is twelve point five, but twelve point five rounds to thirteen, not twelve.
steps.prompt: Why is the upper boundary excluded?
steps.say: The upper boundary is open. Values can get close, but cannot reach it.

steps.name: Write the interval
steps.narration: We write eleven point five is less than or equal to x, and x is less than twelve point five. Keep centimetres as the unit.
steps.prompt: Which inequality symbol is strict?
steps.say: Lower bound included; upper bound excluded. The signs are different.

steps.name: Transfer to another accuracy
steps.narration: The same idea works for decimals and for rounding to ten or one hundred. Change the rounding step, then halve it.
steps.prompt: What changes if a measurement is given to the nearest tenth?
steps.say: For tenths, the halfway margin is zero point zero five. The rule still works.

steps.name: Read the measurement story
steps.narration: A studio desk is two point six metres long. We need its length in centimetres. We start by understanding the units.
steps.prompt: Which unit is recorded, and which unit is wanted?
steps.say: The desk starts in metres. The question wants centimetres.

steps.name: Visualise one metre
steps.narration: One metre contains one hundred centimetres. This is a conversion of length.
steps.prompt: How many centimetres make one metre?
steps.say: Picture one metre split into one hundred centimetres.

steps.name: Choose the factor
steps.narration: To convert metres to centimetres, we multiply by one hundred. That does not change the actual length.
steps.prompt: Should we multiply or divide?
steps.say: The centimetre is smaller, so the numerical count becomes larger.

steps.name: Apply the conversion
steps.narration: Two point six metres is two whole metres and six tenths of a metre. Multiplying by one hundred counts the smaller centimetre units.
steps.prompt: What happens to the value of each digit?
steps.say: Each metre contains one hundred smaller centimetre units.

steps.name: Read the answer with its unit
steps.narration: Two point six times one hundred equals two hundred and sixty. The desk measures two hundred and sixty centimetres.
steps.prompt: What unit belongs with the converted number?
steps.say: Two hundred and sixty centimetres is the same length as two point six metres.

steps.name: Transfer to area and volume
steps.narration: For area, the length scale factor must be squared. For volume, it must be cubed. A squared or cubed unit changes more quickly than a length.
steps.prompt: Why does a square metre contain ten thousand square centimetres?
steps.say: Remember: length times one hundred, area times ten thousand, volume times one million.
